title: A chatbot's bad advice cost Air Canada
summary: A tribunal ordered Air Canada to pay after its chatbot gave a customer wrong advice about bereavement fares.

beats.say: Air Canada's chatbot gave wrong advice. A tribunal made Air Canada pay.
beats.cap: A chatbot's bad advice cost Air Canada

beats.say: A customer asked the chatbot about fares after his grandmother died.
The chatbot said he could claim the discount after flying.
The airline's policy did not allow that.
beats.cap: Policy: no claims after the flight

beats.say: The tribunal ordered damages of about six hundred fifty dollars.
Plus interest, and one hundred twenty five dollars in fees.
The total comes to about eight hundred twelve dollars.
Air Canada argued it was not responsible for what its chatbot said.
beats.cap: Air Canada: not liable for its chatbot

beats.say: The tribunal sent the bill to the airline.
beats.cap: The bill went to the airline

beats.say: One chatbot answer. Eight hundred twelve dollars.

claims.note: Daily Hive: Civil Resolution Tribunal fees of $125

facts.claim: A customer asked Air Canada's chatbot about bereavement fares after his grandmother died, and it said he could apply afterwards
facts.note: Global News: researching flights after his grandmother's death; the chatbot said he could apply for bereavement fares retroactively

facts.claim: Air Canada's policy did not permit retroactive bereavement applications
facts.note: Global News: he later learned Air Canada does not permit retroactive applications

facts.claim: Air Canada argued it could not be held liable for what its chatbot said, and the tribunal disagreed
facts.note: Global News: Air Canada argued it could not be held liable for the information the chatbot provided; the tribunal disagreed

facts.claim: The tribunal ordered damages of $650.88, interest of $36.14 and fees of $125
facts.note: Daily Hive: decision issued February 14, 2024; the three amounts as listed. The $812.02 total is the sum (the article says it is its own calculation)

youtube.hook: Air Canada's chatbot told a customer he could claim a bereavement fare after flying. Air Canada's policy said otherwise. A British Columbia tribunal ordered the airline to pay.
